name: Inverted Channel Ridge Foot
why_habitability: Located at the base of the sinuous ridge on walkable valley floor ground. From this position, astronauts can sample eroded talus and cemented sandstones shedding directly from the inverted riverbed. These deposits record ancient mineral precipitation from liquid water that cemented the stream sediments.
notes: Located at the walkable base of the inverted channel described in HiRISE PSP_006855_1750.

name: East Wall Stratified Outcrop
why_habitability: Finely layered sedimentary bedrock exposed on the lower slopes of the eastern canyon wall. These rhythmic strata record fluctuating water levels and sediment deposition in an ancient lacustrine or groundwater-fed environment. Astronauts can sample across sequential layers to reconstruct climate history.
notes: Stereo observation PSP_007501_1750 documenting canyon wall layering.

name: Debris Levees Overlook
why_habitability: From this vantage point on the eastern terrace, astronauts observe the sinuous debris flow ridge and lateral levees within the canyon below. These mass movements required pore-water saturation and groundwater exfiltration to mobilize down low slopes. Orbital data confirm polyhydrated sulfate signatures in these water-transported deposits.
notes: Walkable terrace overlook observing groundwater-assisted debris levees in the canyon.

name: Canyon Chasm Overlook
why_habitability: An elevated walkable terrace overlook providing clear views of the deep canyon chasm and its exhumed channel floor deposits. From here, astronauts can visually survey and photograph the inverted riverbed and tributary alcoves carved into sulfate strata. It enables comprehensive analysis of fluvial stratigraphy without entering steep, hazardous terrain.
notes: Walkable terrace vantage point overlooking canyon floor debris deposits and strata.

name: Northern Sulfate Terrace and Basin Viewpoint
why_habitability: A broad, level plateau exposure where the layered sulfate unit transitions toward the lower alluvial fan and Gale Crater floor. Astronauts can inspect wind-exhumed sulfate yardangs and evaluate paleoflow vectors as the ancient canyon emptied into the broader basin. This terminal stop provides panoramic context of the entire aqueous depositional system.
notes: Northern terrace viewpoint overlooking the Sakarya Vallis outwash and basin transition.
